title: Availability sets and availability zones for VMs
learningObjective: Deploy VMs into availability sets or zones, explain fault and update domains, and match each option to the failures it survives and its SLA.
foundation: One VM can fail when its server or rack fails, or reboot during maintenance. Running two or more VMs spread out keeps your app up.
An availability set spreads VMs across different racks (fault domains) and maintenance groups (update domains) inside one datacenter.
Availability zones are separate datacenters in a region. Spreading VMs across zones also survives the loss of a whole datacenter.
You choose the set or zone when you create the VM.
engineer: Availability set: up to 3 fault domains (shared power and network; 2 or 3 depending on region) and up to 20 update domains (default 5) that are rebooted one at a time during planned maintenance. Use the Aligned SKU for managed disks so disks follow fault domains. Compute SLA: 99.95% for two or more VMs in a set.

Availability zones: physically separate locations with independent power, cooling and networking. Place VMs in different zones (zones: ['1'], ['2'], ['3']) and use zone-redundant services (Standard Load Balancer, Standard public IP, ZRS disks where supported). SLA: 99.99% for two or more VMs across two or more zones.
Single VM SLA: 99.9% when all disks are Premium SSD, Premium SSD v2 or Ultra (lower for other disk types).

Constraints: a VM's availability set is set at creation (you cannot add an existing VM to a set; recreate it from its disks). A VM cannot be in both an availability set and a zone. Virtual Machine Scale Sets in Flexible mode can spread across zones and fault domains automatically.
Neither option protects against a region-wide outage; use Azure Site Recovery to a second region for that. Proximity placement groups reduce latency, at the cost of spreading.

animation.caption: Open 'Availability sets vs zones': place VMs and inject rack, maintenance, zone and region failures.

example.title: Choosing for an intranet app
body: An intranet app with modest uptime needs runs on two VMs in an availability set (99.95%). A customer-facing checkout service runs three VMs across zones behind a zone-redundant Standard Load Balancer (99.99%).
Both teams also replicate to a paired region with Site Recovery, because neither option protects against regional disasters.

limits: Fault domains up to 3; update domains up to 20
Set or zone chosen at VM creation
portal: Create VM > Availability options: Availability zone (pick zones) or Availability set (create/select).
Availability sets > Create: fault and update domain counts.
configuration.cli:
az vm availability-set create -g rg-app -n avset-web --platform-fault-domain-count 2 --platform-update-domain-count 5
az vm create -g rg-app -n vm-web-1 --image Ubuntu2204 --availability-set avset-web --admin-username azureuser --generate-ssh-keys
az vm create -g rg-app -n vm-web-z1 --image Ubuntu2204 --zone 1 --admin-username azureuser --generate-ssh-keys
az vm create -g rg-app -n vm-web-z2 --image Ubuntu2204 --zone 2 --admin-username azureuser --generate-ssh-keys
configuration.powershell:
New-AzAvailabilitySet -ResourceGroupName rg-app -Name avset-web -Location westeurope -PlatformFaultDomainCount 2 -PlatformUpdateDomainCount 5 -Sku Aligned
New-AzVM -ResourceGroupName rg-app -Name vm-web-z1 -Location westeurope -Image Ubuntu2204 -Zone 1 -Credential (Get-Credential)

lab.objective: Show which placement survives which failure.
steps: Availability set with 4 VMs: inject host failure and maintenance.
Inject a zone failure with the availability set.
Switch to zones with 3 VMs and inject a zone failure, then a region outage.
expected: Only zones survive a datacenter loss
Nothing in one region survives a region outage

validation.text: Survived a zone failure with zones

lab.cost: None. The simulation runs entirely in the browser.

troubleshooting.symptom: Cannot add an existing VM to an availability set.
troubleshooting.cause: Set membership is defined at creation.
troubleshooting.fix: Recreate the VM from its disks in the set.

troubleshooting.symptom: Allocation failure when adding VMs to a set.
troubleshooting.fix: Deallocate all VMs and start them together, or choose another size.

troubleshooting.cause: Region or size has no zone support.

comparisons.difference: EC2 spread placement groups resemble availability sets; deploying across AZs resembles Azure zones.
Automate spreading across zones and fault domains with autoscale.

misconceptions.myth: An availability set protects against datacenter failure.
misconceptions.reality: It spreads across racks in one datacenter.

misconceptions.myth: A single VM in a zone gets 99.99%.
misconceptions.reality: 99.99% needs two or more VMs across zones.

architectureDecisions: Use zones for business-critical tiers when the region supports them.
Pair VM redundancy with zone-redundant load balancing and storage.
Add a second region for disaster recovery.

walkthrough.subtitle: Keep an app running when hardware fails or Azure updates its servers.

steps.label: Single VM
steps.title: One VM is one point of failure
body: A failed host, a power problem in a rack, or a planned update can take the only VM down.

steps.label: Domains
steps.title: Two kinds of failure
body: Fault domains are groups of hardware that share power and network (racks). Update domains are groups that Azure restarts together during planned maintenance.

steps.label: Sets
steps.title: Availability sets spread VMs in one datacenter
body: VMs in an availability set are spread over up to 3 fault domains and up to 20 update domains. Two or more VMs in a set get a 99.95% SLA.
You choose the set when you create the VM; you cannot add an existing VM later.

callout.text: An availability set does not protect against a whole datacenter failing.

steps.label: Zones
steps.title: Availability zones spread VMs across buildings
body: Zones are separate datacenters in a region with their own power, cooling and network. VMs in two or more zones get a 99.99% SLA. Put a load balancer in front to spread traffic.

steps.label: Choose
steps.title: Choosing
body: Need the highest protection in one region: zones. Region without zones, or apps needing very low latency between VMs: availability set. A single VM with Premium SSD disks gets 99.9%.

steps.label: Recap
steps.title: Availability
body: Spread copies so one failure cannot stop you.
recap: Fault domain = shared hardware; update domain = maintenance group
Add a load balancer in front

handsOn.title: Explore availability options without paying for VMs
handsOn.cost: Free. You create an empty availability set and only look at the VM form.
before: Signed in at portal.azure.com as Owner of a subscription (a free or pay-as-you-go account works). Work in a resource group called rg-az104-lab.
If rg-az104-lab does not exist yet: search 'Resource groups' > Create > name rg-az104-lab, region UAE North (or any region near you) > Review + create > Create.

steps.do: Search 'Availability sets' > + Create. Group: rg-az104-lab, name: avset-lab, fault domains: 2, update domains: 5. Create.
steps.see: avset-lab created. It contains no VMs and costs nothing.

steps.do: Open Virtual machines > + Create > Azure virtual machine. Open the 'Availability options' list.
steps.see: No infrastructure redundancy required, Availability zone, Virtual machine scale set, Availability set.

steps.do: Choose Availability zone and tick zones 1, 2 and 3.
steps.see: A message that one VM will be created in each selected zone.

steps.do: Choose Availability set and pick avset-lab.
steps.see: The VM would be placed in your set. Do not create it.

steps.do: Cancel the form. Open avset-lab > Overview.
steps.see: Fault and update domain counts. There is no button to add an existing VM.

check: You found where zones and sets are chosen, and saw that sets are chosen at VM creation.
cleanup: When you finish for the day: Resource groups > rg-az104-lab > Delete resource group > type the name > Delete. This removes everything inside it.
